title: spawn mission configure changes only what it is given: settings merge into the current ones, clearing is an explicit switch, and the output and the record show the whole result
prompt:
Read, in crates/spawn-cli/src/missions.rs, `USAGE`, `Settings` (`Settings::from`: an omitted --accept becomes `review`, an omitted --gate, --minutes, --tool-calls, --backlog/--resident or --workers becomes nothing; `apply`) and the `configure` and `add` verbs (configure prints `{mission, gate, accept, objectives}`, the settings it was given); `Flags::parse` in crates/spawn-cli/src/config.rs (every flag takes a value); `mission_configure` in crates/spawn-postgres; in crates/spawn-postgres/sql/schema.sql `spawn_mission_configure` (its checks, under the append lock, then the `mission.configured` record of exactly what it was given) and the fold of `mission.configured` in `spawn_control_apply` (it overwrites gate, accept, budget and objectives); who reads those columns (crates/spawn-cli/src/integrate.rs: `Mission`, `enforce_budget`, `objectives::assign_next`; crates/spawn-cli/src/serve.rs); docs/fleet-architecture.md §3.2 and §10.3-§10.4 and docs/design.md §14.

The problem. `spawn mission configure --id N <settings>` stores the whole configuration from the flags of that one call. A call meant to change one number, `spawn mission configure --id 4 --tool-calls 300`, would switch mission 4 (the RSI mission: accept by gate, a 150-minute and 300-call budget, the controller's backlog, resident rsi, 3 workers) to review-landing and drop its gate, its minutes and its backlog: the integrator stops landing it and stops assigning objectives, silently, since the command succeeds and prints only what it was given. So every configure restates every setting: mission 4 has been configured 8 times since 2026-11-04, each call repeating all seven settings to change one or two (on 2026-11-06 at 05:14:41 UTC only the budget, 90 minutes and 150 calls to 150 and 300), and one forgotten flag is a silent outage. The owner's goal (2026-11-06) is the Pareto frontier: no dimension improves by letting another regress; this costs autonomy and reliability for nothing.

Required behaviour (the contract the gate checks).
1. Configure merges. `spawn mission configure --id N` changes only the settings it is given and keeps every other as the mission has it: --gate, --accept, each budget field (--minutes, --tool-calls) and each objectives field (--backlog, --resident, --workers) on its own. Objectives given for a mission that has none need --backlog and --resident (as today); for one that has them, any one field may be given alone.
2. Clearing is explicit. A setting is cleared only by its own switch, which takes no value: --no-gate, --no-budget (both fields), --no-minutes, --no-tool-calls, --no-objectives, --no-workers (back to the default 1). A switch and a value for the same setting in one call is refused. --accept goes back to review only when given (`--accept review`). The checks on the result are today's: objectives need a gate (so --no-gate on a mission with objectives is refused unless --no-objectives is in the same call), a gate is an absolute directory, workers 1 to 16, a gate only on a local source. A refused call changes nothing.
3. The merge is the database's. The CLI sends what it was given and what it clears; `spawn_mission_configure` merges them into the mission's row as it is under the append lock, checks the result and records it, so two configures never lose each other's change and no caller can store a configuration it did not read (the CLI is the only caller today, with integrate.rs's tests; keep them working).
4. It says what changed. configure prints JSON `{"mission": N, "before": {...}, "after": {...}}`, each with gate, accept, budget and objectives, before as the mission had them and after as recorded. A call that sets nothing changes nothing and records nothing (before = after).
5. The record is the whole result. `mission.configured` holds the whole resulting configuration (gate, accept, budget, objectives), not the flags of the call, so the fold, which overwrites the four columns, stays right, and the record alone says what the mission was configured to from then on.
6. Causality (§14): the result is computed from the mission's row read under the lock that records it, never from what the caller believes the mission holds.

How the saving shows, in numbers. A configure names only what it changes: `--tool-calls 300` instead of seven flags; no silent loss of a gate, a budget or a backlog, which would stop a mission's landings and objectives until someone noticed. On 017's scorecard: autonomy and reliability no worse (a mission never stops because a configure forgot a flag), and nothing else moves.

State the rule in missions.rs's `USAGE` and module comment, in docs/fleet-architecture.md §10.3 and in schema.sql beside `spawn_mission_configure`. Add unit tests: `Settings` parses the clearing switches and refuses a switch with a value for the same setting; a switch takes no value while every other flag still needs one. In crates/spawn-postgres/tests/: the merge of each setting alone, each clearing switch, the refusals (objectives without a gate, a switch and a value together) leaving the row and the log unchanged, a call that sets nothing recording nothing, and the record holding the whole result.

The gate judges this with rsi/scenarios/027.sh (read it: its header lists today's measures). No loop and no integrator: one mission on a local source, configured in full first (--gate <dir> --accept gate --minutes 45 --tool-calls 60 --backlog <dir> --resident rsi --workers 3), then read from mission_missions and its records after each call. It checks:
- (1) `configure --id N --tool-calls 200`: budget.tool_calls is 200, and gate, accept, budget.minutes and objectives are what they were;
- (2) its output's `before` and `after` are the configuration before and after the call;
- (3) the newest `mission.configured` record holds the whole resulting configuration;
- (4) `--workers 2` changes objectives.workers alone; `--minutes 90` changes budget.minutes alone;
- (5) `--no-budget` clears the budget and nothing else; `--no-gate` while objectives are set is refused and changes nothing; `--no-objectives` clears the objectives and nothing else; `--no-gate --accept review` then clears the gate;
- (6) `configure --id N` with no setting changes nothing.
On the live main (49b92be; the deployed binary is built from it) it fails at (1): "(1) `spawn mission configure --id 1 --tool-calls 200` changed more than the tool-call budget: the mission is now {"gate": null, "accept": "review", "budget": {"tool_calls": 200}, "objectives": null}, was {"gate": "<dir>", "accept": "gate", "budget": {"minutes": 45, "tool_calls": 60}, "objectives": {"backlog": "<dir>", "workers": 3, "resident": "rsi"}}". A stand-in that merges as above passes every check. It runs in about 11 s. It exits 0 when every check passes, 1 when an assertion fails, 2 on a harness failure.

Rules: never edit the protected paths, which the gate rejects: rsi/, scripts/ (scripts/rsi/, scripts/blackbox/, scripts/e2e.sh among them), deploy/, all of web/ except web/src/ and web/index.html, rust-toolchain files and .cargo/. The gate also rejects fewer runnable tests than the base (do not delete, rename, ignore or disable tests), any lint relaxation ([lints] tables, clippy.toml, a new crate-level #![allow]/#![expect], a removed #![warn]/#![deny]) and any build-time code (build.rs, .cargo/, a `build =` key in a Cargo.toml). The gate builds offline from the cargo caches already on the host: a new crate builds only if it is already in ~/.cargo/registry. Keep every existing check green (clippy -D warnings, the workspace tests, the e2e, the black-box scenarios, the web build) and add tests of your own for the new behaviour.
